parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists discuss the same global temperature shock and GDP study: global temperature shocks, local projections over 10-year horizons, roughly 50–60 annual observations, scaling to 1°C, SCC and welfare translation, and lag choices in shock construction.

pairs.reason: Both say historical shocks are small (about 0.3°C), so linear extrapolation to 1°C or more, and the treatment of nonlinearities, is weakly supported. A1 also bundles lag-length and growth-versus-level concerns.

Both concern the lag order used in the temperature shock construction. A1 asks for more lags to capture long geophysical cycles, while B1 says the h/p choices are not uniquely grounded and embed persistence assumptions.

Both question whether the reported standard errors and confidence regions are valid. A2 points to few observations and many parameters and asks for simulation evidence; B2 points to overlapping long-horizon local-projection outcomes and persistent regressors.

Both question the validity of the inference behind the main confidence intervals. A5 cites asymptotics with about 50 observations and 7 or more parameters; B2 cites overlapping long-horizon local-projection outcomes and persistence.
Both concern the confidence bands. A2 asks whether the bands are statistically valid in small samples, while B6 says they omit model and extrapolation uncertainty.
Both concern the confidence intervals, but A5 is about small-sample asymptotics and B6 is about omitted sources of uncertainty.

Both concern long-run damages beyond the 10-year horizon and the SCC. A3 asks for longer-horizon effects to be estimated, while B5 objects that the damage-kernel functional form extrapolates beyond the observed horizons and that the welfare model is restrictive.
Both touch on how persistence and long-run damage are mapped into welfare. B4 focuses on temperature persistence driving the 12% figure, while A3 asks for longer horizons.
B6 mentions long-horizon extrapolation uncertainty, but the mechanism differs from A3's request for estimates beyond 10 years.
Both note the small annual sample. B11 uses it to argue that confounding cannot be ruled out, whereas A6 calls for more data and robustness checks in general.
Both mention roughly 50–60 annual observations, but A5 concerns asymptotic inference and B11 concerns confounding by global shocks.
Both relate to small sample size; A4 notes that the longer BU sample and bootstrapping address it, while B11 raises confounding.
